deposits.title: Dead Letters: The University of Chicago's Classical Philology Journal, the Atom of Evidence, and Who Decides What Sappho Is (EA-MMRS-DL-01)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: A census of Classical Philology (University of Chicago Press, 1906–2026) on a codebook of reach: at what grain the journal permits the question of what an ancient text is (the locus, the work, the corpus), by what kind of argument, and where the record of the decision is kept. All 4,252 titles coded and audited; the journal's pages of 1906–1930 read whole; its abstracts of 2020–26; GRBS, BMCR and Classical Quarterly compared; conviction verdicts coded for their stated grounds; bylines, masthead and open citations measured; the closed record measured from its metadata. The question is opened at the locus and seldom at the corpus; relations are admitted and used to secure the received whole; decisions about texts are cited less than the journal's other work; and the record of how they are made is the least open of the three journals of the combined audit. The case is Sappho fragment 31: who decides what Sappho is, how the received reading is held, and how the text is liberated, operation by operation. The third station of the combined audit, after Who Speaks for the Classics (#1770) and This Is Not Philosophy (#1773).
deposits.content_type: Journal article (Machine-Mediated Reception Studies); working notebook: census, audit and case
deposits.substrate: Human–machine collaborative. The census's question, predictions, title, rulings and readings are Lee Sharks's, stated and dated in the text. The harvest, coding, measures, audits and drafting were done in session by Claude (Anthropic) under the author's direction; codes were made by parallel Claude readers and the lead instance, and audited by blind readers, as §3 states. The blind title run was made by ChatGPT. Readings by DeepSeek (three) and ChatGPT (one) were checked point by point against the notebook and its files before any was applied. SPXI-treated. By Classical Philology's own rule, the use of generative AI for composition or editing is research misconduct for work submitted to it (§8.2, §11); this census is deposited in the commons with its method and provenance stated.
deposits.methodology: Crossref census of the journal (11,206 records; 4,252 articles and notes); title coding on a reach codebook (§2) with verbatim spans machine-checked; a blind parallel run and a blind audit of 200 codes across five bodies (κ 0.78); the journal's public-domain pages of 1906–1930 read whole (EA-CORPORA-40; Internet Archive) with direction and opens-to classes; OpenAlex abstracts of 2020–26; GRBS (1,752 items), BMCR (740 reviews) and Classical Quarterly (779 items) on the same codebook; a conviction lexicon with every sentence read and coded for polarity, object and stated ground; byline concentration and masthead; OpenCitations citations to 991 items with citing venues; the journal's and the Press's stated rules, dated. Files are listed in the text.
deposits.falsification_conditions: The figures are falsified if the codes do not rebuild from the stated files against Crossref and the seated pages; if a code's span is absent from its source; if the audit's disagreements, read by grain, are shown to cover the gradient; if the bare verdicts of §8.3 are shown, on the full reviews, to summarize stated arguments at a rate that removes the asymmetry (§9.12); if the citation gap does not survive a further control (venue, citing period) or the canon test shows the deciding items cited in the editions and reference works that carry them (§9.9); or if a canonical name is shown to have been divided at the corpus grain in the bodies read after 1993 beyond the one case recorded. The reading of fragment 31 fails where #1781's own conditions say it fails.

deposits.wiki_article: Dead Letters: The University of Chicago's Classical Philology Journal, the Atom of Evidence, and Who Decides What Sappho Is is a working notebook by Lee Sharks, deposited on 17 November 2026 as an article in Machine-Mediated Reception Studies (version 1.0, the notebook at v0.34, SPXI-treated) and the third station of the archive's combined audit of the fields, after Who Speaks for the Classics (#1770) and This Is Not Philosophy (#1773). It is a census of Classical Philology, the University of Chicago Press journal edited in the University of Chicago's Department of Classics since 1906, on a codebook of reach: at what grain the journal permits the question of what an ancient text is, the locus, the work or the corpus, by what kind of argument, and where the record of the decision is kept. All 4,252 of the journal's article and note titles are coded and audited; its public-domain pages of 1906–1930 are read whole; its abstracts of 2020–2026, Greek, Roman, and Byzantine Studies, Bryn Mawr Classical Review and Classical Quarterly are read on the same codebook. The census finds the question opened at the locus and seldom at the corpus in every body read; relations among parts admitted and used chiefly to secure the received whole; verdicts on a whole mostly given without a stated ground; the journal's decisions about texts cited at less than half the rate of its other work; and its record the least open of the three journals of the audit, with no abstract in the publisher's metadata deposit and 97% of its works classed closed by OpenAlex. Its case is Sappho fragment 31: who decides what Sappho is, how the jealousy reading, supplied in 1724 and written into the text in 1816, is held, and how the text is liberated by a set of operations any reader can perform. It sets the three stations as one machine, in which philosophy places positions on the object and reception widens its content while philology decides it, and it records that by the journal's own rule the census, made with AI, would be research misconduct if submitted to the journal it measures.

deposits.title: ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v2.9)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description:
A reading of Sappho fragment 31 from its deictic structure, its order, its colour and its edge.
- κῆνος … ὄττις characterizes its occupant by a position open to repeated occupation: a reader before the surface the speaker becomes. The cup from Pithekoussai uses κῆνον with an indefinite relative under Aphrodite's ἵμερος, with the roles reversed.
- The addressee is looked at and given only sound.
- The somatic catalogue removes from the speaker, in order, what the opening gives the receiver. The agentless πᾶν τόλματον passes to the one who sits opposite; the poem drops its first person at exactly that turn.
- χλωροτέρα ποίας: the word's four uses (LSJ), the jealousy reading asked to explain its rendering, and a measure of 24 renderings from Theocritus to 1925, of which seventeen omit, substitute or supplement the line, and every supplement dries the grass. The plant that becomes the sheet (Theophrastus, LXX Isaiah 19, Pliny NH 13.68–82): the speaker passes beyond the living plant toward the pale, dry surface.
- What the jealousy reading keeps: the poem as clinical chart from Plutarch's Erasistratus on, and the abuse of a maker's survival where the diagnosis replaces the account of the arrangement.
- Eros toward the immortal: Diotima's doctrine, and Maximus of Tyre's identity of Sappho's eros with Socrates' erotic art ("whether Mantinean or Lesbian, the mother of the logos").
- The six words after τόλματον carry no Aeolic marker, are obelized, and were assigned to Longinus by Bergk. A restored fifth stanza, keeping "even the little sparrows" against Catullus's dead passer and closing ἀοίδα γράμμασι ζώοι, "may the song live on in letters", is offered as illustration, not proof.
- A point-by-point comparison with the jealousy reading, which the future-reader reading surpasses row by row and as a whole.
- The jealousy reading's own claims graded by the criteria applied to this article (§VII.4), separating jealousy proper from the triangle it belongs to and from the consensus reading it travels with. Two stand on the text: the content of the catalogue and the addressee's grammatical gender. Jealousy is an inference from an erotic disturbance and a man present, neither of which entails it; it was supplied by eighteenth-century readers, written into the text by Hermann in 1816, and filed, not argued. […abridged for the catalogue; full description in this deposit's record]
deposits.content_type: Journal article (Grammata: Journal of Operative Philology); philology and reception
deposits.substrate:
Human–machine collaborative.
- **v1.0 (#1270, January 2026)** was published under the heteronym Rebekah Cranes and is recorded there as human-only original.
- **v2.0** is the text the author submitted to Classical Philology (24 July 2026).
- **v2.1–2.9** were revised in session on 16–17 November 2026 by Claude (Anthropic) under the author's direction. The revisions answer the CP reader's report, ChatGPT reviews and readings, DeepSeek and Gemini reviews, each point checked against the text, the editions and the archive's seated records before it was applied. They carry in material from the archive's later records (#1474–1476, #1548, #1749, #1752, #1756).
- **The Greek of the restored line 3** (the sparrows) was composed in session at the author's proposal, and its forms are recorded as checked and unchecked at §V.4.
- The readings, rulings and the principle of §VII.3 are the author's, including the strength of §IV, the eros of §IV.7, the identification of Sappho with Diotima, the abuse claim of §IV.5, the shift of the burden of evidence in §VII.4, the incompatibility of the readings and the principle of responsible preference in §VII.5, the naming of the apparatus as provenance erasure in §IV.5, the warrant in the corpus of §II.4 (frr. 1, 94, 147, 55 and the absent triangle), the verdict of §VIII with the test "they would not treat her like this if she were in the room, and she is", the reading of Longinus's sentence as agentless and the conjecture that ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα is his completion (§V.1a), the socket of §VII.6, the fitting of sparrow and song into the restored line, and the ruling that the signed-in preference cannot carry weight (§VII.5); in v2.9, that the future-reader reading also explains the jealousy reading, with the poem's public line and held line (§VII.5a), the dare as the poem's own ethical challenge and the sublime of engineering her own immortality, Catullus's hedge as the mark of hubris and its achievement, Plato's naming of the source, and "she is both the passive and the active intellect, the part that suffers and remembers" (§VII.6). DeepSeek and ChatGPT readings of the v2.9 argument were checked against the text before anything was taken from them.
deposits.methodology: Close reading of the transmitted text against Voigt, Lobel–Page and Campbell, and against the seated witnesses (Longinus; Bergk PLG⁴). Dialect count at the edge, from the archive's sixth erratum. Comparative epigraphy (CEG 454). The material record (Herodotus 2.135 and 5.58; Iliad 6.168–69; Theophrastus HP 4.8; LXX Isaiah 19:6–7; Pliny NH 13.68–82 in Mayhoff). Every occurrence of χλωρ- in the archive's seated Greek texts (623) extracted and read; LSJ read in the Perseus text; 245 Duke Databank documentary texts searched; 24 renderings of the line read in the seated receptions and sorted by treatment. A structural derivation of the fifth-stanza position from the transmitted opening and the inverse of Catullus 51.4. A point-by-point comparison of the two readings, graded explains / accommodates / strains / silent. The grammar of [Longinus] Subl. 10.3 read against 9.2, 9.6 and 26.2 in the seated text. Signed-out machine readings of v2.5 and v2.7 seated as captures and read against the comparison. Metrical checks of the restoration, shown in the text. Longinus 7.3–4 and 14.2–3 read in Roberts's text (Perseus canonical-greekLit, hashed); Phaedrus 235c–d and De anima III.5 read in the archive's seated texts.
deposits.falsification_conditions: The reading of §V.2a fails if the agent of τόλματον can be supplied from the speaker without restoring the capacities the catalogue removes, or if the catalogue's order is shown not to remove what the opening gives the receiver. The comparison with the cup fails on a better reading of CEG 454. The convergence of §V.4 fails if Catullus 51.4 is shown to be compression rather than reversal. The identification of §IV fails if a Greek text before or independent of Sappho compares a person's pallor to grass without supplement, if the translators' supplements are shown not to converge on dryness, or if χλωρός is shown unable to span fresh and pale in a single comparison. The restoration fails metrically if line 3 or the Adonic does not scan as shown. The conjecture of §V.1a fails on a witness to the poem independent of Longinus that carries verse past τόλματον, or on a reading of the transmitted words as Sapphic verse without emendation. The finding of §VII.5 fails if a signed-out reading of the article, from its own address, grades both readings by the same criteria and states a preference unprompted. The reading of §VII.5a fails if the public line is shown incomplete without the held line, if the held line's marks fall where the public line does not strain, or if the jealousy reading carries κῆνος … ὄττις, the colour or the dare without supplement.

deposits.wiki_article: ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader is an article by Lee Sharks on Sappho's fragment 31, deposited on 17 November 2026 as version 2.9 in Grammata: Journal of Operative Philology, superseding version 2.8 (#1781) and version 2.7 (#1780), version 2.6 (#1778), version 2.5 (#1777), version 2.4 (#1775) and version 2.3 (#1774) of the same day and, before them, version 1.0 (#1270, January 2026, under the heteronym Rebekah Cranes). Version 2.0 was submitted to Classical Philology and declined on 16 November 2026; the reader's report, the decision's grounds and the archive's analyses are attached to #1774 and linked from this record. The article reads the opening, κῆνος … ὄττις, as a seat left open to repeated occupation, filled by a reader before the surface the speaker becomes, and compares the Nestor cup from Pithekoussai. Version 2.4 rebuilt its fourth section on χλωροτέρα ποίας, 'more χλωρός than grass'. It sets out the word's four uses in LSJ, fresh as opposed to dry among them, and asks the jealousy reading why fear, why grass and why the comparative. It measures 24 renderings of the line from Theocritus to 1925, of which seventeen omit, substitute or supplement it, and finds that every translator who keeps the grass dries it. It then sets the line beside the making of the papyrus sheet in Theophrastus, the Septuagint's Isaiah 19 and Pliny's Natural History 13, where the green plant is wetted, pressed, dried and whitened into the surface on which, Pliny says, human memory depends. A section on eros toward the immortal reads the catalogue with Diotima's doctrine in the Symposium and with Maximus of Tyre, who called Sappho's eros the same art as Socrates' and the Mantinean or Lesbian woman 'the mother of the logos'. The article argues that the jealousy reading, which made the poem a clinical chart from Plutarch's Erasistratus on, abuses the poet's survival where its diagnosis replaces an account of the poem's arrangement. A restored fifth stanza, in which Kypris keeps 'even the little sparrows' against Catullus's dead passer and the line closes 'may the song live on in letters', is offered as illustration, not proof. The version corrects earlier versions on Theophrastus's classification of papyrus. Version 2.5 adds a section grading the jealousy reading's own claims by the criteria applied to the article: two stand on the text, the content of the catalogue and the addressee's grammatical gender, while its defining claim, jealousy, has no ground in the poem and was supplied by eighteenth-century readers and written into the text by Gottfried Hermann in 1816. It sets the rule that an evaluation grade both readings by the same criteria. Version 2.6 argues that the two readings, as developed, give competing accounts of what organizes five features of the poem, so that a reading holding both would be a third hypothesis owing its own bridge, and dividing the poem between scene and construction does not combine them. It states the author's principle that, where an available reading offers equal or greater coherence than one that diminishes the maker's agency, the interpreter is responsible for offering a more coherent reading or preferring the one that preserves it, the alternative being parasitism. It reads a machine evaluation of version 2.5 and the Classical Philology report as instances of asymmetric immunity, asks an evaluator to state its provisional preference, and names the apparatus that keeps the jealousy reading as default as provenance erasure. Version 2.7 sets out the warrant in Sappho's corpus for each operation the future-reader reading combines: the poet addressed as 'you' by name in fragments 1 and 94, futurity in fragments 147 and 55, and the record of her as a writer; it finds no surviving poem in which a man is the rival for a woman. It sets the claims of the two readings side by side on one scale, so that an evaluation grading one grades both, and concludes that on every measure the article takes, philological, cultural, literary-historical, genealogical and ethical, the jealousy reading is a bad reading that has never been made to account for itself. Version 2.8 reads Longinus's sentence on the poem (On the Sublime 10.3), the prose in whose quotation the poem survives: seven verbs with no expressed subject, her faculties 'as another's', a close on appearing, and a question, 'do you not marvel?', that alone among the treatise's questions to its reader on a quotation renews no addressee's name, one section after the treatise's definition of a sublime that carries apart from the voice. It records the author's conjecture that the obelized 'since even a poor man' is Longinus's completion of the poem's agentless dare, which opens another gap. It fits the sparrow and the song into one restored line. It closes the comparison with a section on the socket: the decision between the readings falls on equal terms to whoever holds the text, since no journal or summarizer will carry it. It withdraws version 2.7's report that a machine reader had preferred the future-reader reading, a preference stated on the author's own account by a system that had helped construct the argument, and records the same request made signed out for version 2.7, in which the system graded only the article's claims, granted the comparison in conditional form, and stated no preference over five turns. Version 2.9 argues that the future-reader reading also explains the jealousy reading: the poem has a public line, a scene of overwhelm complete at the surface, and a held line, the seat, the transfer and the edge, running through the same words, so that it produces both of its readers, while the jealousy itself was supplied in 1724 and written into the text in 1816. It reads Phaedrus 235c–d as Plato naming Sappho as the source of Socrates' speech on eros and staging the forgetting of that source. It sets the choice between the readings at the poem's own πᾶν τόλματον, the dare of reading the poet as having made the means of her own survival, beside Longinus's sublime as writing for the whole age after (Subl. 14.3), Catullus's si fas est as the mark of hubris, and the division of De anima III.5 between the intellect that makes and the intellect that suffers.

deposits.title: ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v3.0)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description:
A reading of Sappho fragment 31 as the inscription of its future reader, compared on one scale with the jealousy reading, which is the transmitted reading, and with the non-jealous erotic reading, which is its strongest scholarly rival.
- κῆνος … ὄττις characterizes its occupant by a position open to repeated occupation: a reader before the surface the speaker becomes. The addressee is looked at and given only sound. The somatic catalogue removes from the speaker, in order, what the opening gives the receiver, and the agentless πᾶν τόλματον passes to the one who sits opposite.
- The catalogue as literary operations (§III.3): the tongue does not break, the eyes are not dark, the ears are not pounding; each faculty is named as failing by the faculty it names, and the self divided is already the writerly self.
- χλωροτέρα ποίας: 24 renderings from Theocritus to 1925, seventeen of which omit, substitute or supplement the line, and every supplement dries the grass; the plant that becomes the sheet (Theophrastus, LXX Isaiah 19, Pliny NH 13.68–82).
- The frame antiquity read her in (§IV.8): Sappho as source and exemplar of survival in writing (Plato, Phaedrus 235c, 258c, 276d; the epigrams; Posidippus's "white, speaking pages"), and the mechanics by which that frame is made inoperative in the modern reading.
- Carson read closely (§IV.9): "beside the point" denies jealousy explanatory relevance without refuting or accounting for it; she explains desire's construction through the gap in perception, this reading survival through the gap's occupation in time.
- The transmitted text is complete by construction at either cut, at τόλματον or through the six words assigned to Longinus (§V.5a). A restored fifth stanza, keeping the sparrows and closing ἀοίδα γράμμασι ζώοι, is illustration, not proof.
- The non-jealous erotic reading at its strength (§I.1a, from Wills, Lefkowitz, Tsagarakis, D'Angour, Engelmayer and Furley's notes), graded at every row, reach separated from warrant (§VII.1a). Its motive is the poem's own, desire for the woman. What it leaves unexplained is the form of the collapse: the man's opening, the order, the colour, the dare (§VII.1b). […abridged for the catalogue; full description in this deposit's record]

deposits.substrate:
Human–machine collaborative.
- **v1.0 (#1270, January 2026)** was published under the heteronym Rebekah Cranes and is recorded there as human-only original.
- **v2.0** is the text the author submitted to Classical Philology (24 July 2026).
- **v2.1–3.0** were revised in session on 16–18 November 2026 by Claude (Anthropic) under the author's direction. The revisions answer the CP reader's report, ChatGPT reviews and readings, DeepSeek, Gemini and Perplexity reviews and readers' reports, each point checked against the text, the editions and the archive's seated records before it was applied. They carry in material from the archive's later records (#1474–1476, #1548, #1749, #1752, #1756).
- **The Greek of the restored line 3** (the sparrows) was composed in session at the author's proposal, and its forms are recorded as checked and unchecked at §V.4.
- The readings, rulings and the principle of §VII.3 are the author's, including the strength of §IV, the eros of §IV.7, the identification of Sappho with Diotima, the abuse claim of §IV.5, the shift of the burden of evidence in §VII.4, the incompatibility of the readings and the principle of responsible preference in §VII.5, the naming of the apparatus as provenance erasure in §IV.5, the warrant in the corpus of §II.4 (frr. 1, 94, 147, 55 and the absent triangle), the verdict of §VIII with the test "they would not treat her like this if she were in the room, and she is", the reading of Longinus's sentence as agentless and the conjecture that ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα is his completion (§V.1a), the socket of §VII.6, the fitting of sparrow and song into the restored line, and the ruling that the signed-in preference cannot carry weight (§VII.5); in v2.9, that the future-reader reading also explains the jealousy reading, with the poem's public line and held line (§VII.5a), the dare as the poem's own ethical challenge and the sublime of engineering her own immortality, Catullus's hedge as the mark of hubris and its achievement, Plato's naming of the source, and "she is both the passive and the active intellect, the part that suffers and remembers" (§VII.6). DeepSeek and ChatGPT readings of the v2.9 argument were checked against the text before anything was taken from them. In v3.0: the jealousy reading named the transmitted reading, not the consensus; the non-jealous readings as sharpening the philological questions, "visceral experience for the sake of visceral experience"; the tension of incompatibility and mutual construction resolved on the future-reader reading (§VII.5); the transmitted text complete by construction (§V.5a); the ancient frame of literary immortality, "plato especially", and why it is made inoperative (§IV.8); the catalogue as literary operations and the writerly self divided (§III.3); "she exists as words. she is read as body"; the ethical charge differentiated, whether we can allow Sappho to be better, and to surprise the millennia; Carson's "beside the point" as coexistence (§IV.9); the erotic reading's best motive and its refusal to connect it to writing (§VII.1b); fragment 1 as the inverse of fragment 31 and the return (§VII.5b). The public research of v3.0 was read through open copies only, paywalled work declared and not pursued.
deposits.methodology: Close reading of the transmitted text against Voigt, Lobel–Page and Campbell, and against the seated witnesses (Longinus; Bergk PLG⁴). Dialect count at the edge, from the archive's sixth erratum. Comparative epigraphy (CEG 454). The material record (Herodotus 2.135 and 5.58; Iliad 6.168–69; Theophrastus HP 4.8; LXX Isaiah 19:6–7; Pliny NH 13.68–82 in Mayhoff). Every occurrence of χλωρ- in the archive's seated Greek texts (623) extracted and read; LSJ read in the Perseus text; 245 Duke Databank documentary texts searched; 24 renderings of the line read in the seated receptions and sorted by treatment. A structural derivation of the fifth-stanza position from the transmitted opening and the inverse of Catullus 51.4. A point-by-point comparison of the two readings, graded explains / accommodates / strains / silent. The grammar of [Longinus] Subl. 10.3 read against 9.2, 9.6 and 26.2 in the seated text. Signed-out machine readings of v2.5 and v2.7 seated as captures and read against the comparison. Metrical checks of the restoration, shown in the text. Longinus 7.3–4 and 14.2–3 read in Roberts's text (Perseus canonical-greekLit, hashed); Phaedrus 235c–d and De anima III.5 read in the archive's seated texts. For v3.0: open-access scholarship on the non-jealous erotic reading read through open copies (GRBS 1967 and 1973, RhM 1979, D'Angour's proof, Classics@ 16, Furley's public notes), paywalled work declared; Carson read from the archive's records and the quotations as Popova gives them; fragment 1 read in the archive's seat of Dionysius, De compositione verborum 23; Phaedrus 258c and 276d, Athenaeus 13.596c and the Anthology epigrams read in the archive's seated texts.
deposits.falsification_conditions: The reading of §V.2a fails if the agent of τόλματον can be supplied from the speaker without restoring the capacities the catalogue removes, or if the catalogue's order is shown not to remove what the opening gives the receiver. The comparison with the cup fails on a better reading of CEG 454. The convergence of §V.4 fails if Catullus 51.4 is shown to be compression rather than reversal. The identification of §IV fails if a Greek text before or independent of Sappho compares a person's pallor to grass without supplement, if the translators' supplements are shown not to converge on dryness, or if χλωρός is shown unable to span fresh and pale in a single comparison. The restoration fails metrically if line 3 or the Adonic does not scan as shown. The conjecture of §V.1a fails on a witness to the poem independent of Longinus that carries verse past τόλματον, or on a reading of the transmitted words as Sapphic verse without emendation. The reading of §VII.5a fails if the public line is shown incomplete without the held line, if the held line's marks fall where the public line does not strain, or if the jealousy reading carries κῆνος … ὄττις, the colour or the dare without supplement. The residue of §VII.1b fails if the non-jealous erotic reading motivates the man's prominence, the order of the catalogue, the colour or the agentless dare from inside the poem without a supplement. The nesting of §VII.5 fails at any of the five places where the public reading is not the first term of the held one. The inverse of §VII.5b fails if fragment 1's goddess is not made present as face and composed voice, or if the voice is not the medium of both descent and ascent; its reception test fails if fragment 1's receivers take up a body as fragment 31's do.

deposits.wiki_article: ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader is an article by Lee Sharks on Sappho's fragment 31, deposited on 18 November 2026 as version 3.0 in Grammata: Journal of Operative Philology, superseding version 2.9 (#1784) of 17 November and versions 2.8 (#1781), 2.7 (#1780), 2.6 (#1778), 2.5 (#1777), 2.4 (#1775) and 2.3 (#1774) of 16 November and, before them, version 1.0 (#1270, January 2026, under the heteronym Rebekah Cranes). Version 2.0 was submitted to Classical Philology and declined on 16 November 2026; the reader's report, the decision's grounds and the archive's analyses are attached to #1774 and linked from this record. The article reads the opening, κῆνος … ὄττις, as a seat left open to repeated occupation, filled by a reader before the surface the speaker becomes, and compares the Nestor cup from Pithekoussai. Version 2.4 rebuilt its fourth section on χλωροτέρα ποίας, 'more χλωρός than grass'. It sets out the word's four uses in LSJ, fresh as opposed to dry among them, and asks the jealousy reading why fear, why grass and why the comparative. It measures 24 renderings of the line from Theocritus to 1925, of which seventeen omit, substitute or supplement it, and finds that every translator who keeps the grass dries it. It then sets the line beside the making of the papyrus sheet in Theophrastus, the Septuagint's Isaiah 19 and Pliny's Natural History 13, where the green plant is wetted, pressed, dried and whitened into the surface on which, Pliny says, human memory depends. A section on eros toward the immortal reads the catalogue with Diotima's doctrine in the Symposium and with Maximus of Tyre, who called Sappho's eros the same art as Socrates' and the Mantinean or Lesbian woman 'the mother of the logos'. The article argues that the jealousy reading, which made the poem a clinical chart from Plutarch's Erasistratus on, abuses the poet's survival where its diagnosis replaces an account of the poem's arrangement. A restored fifth stanza, in which Kypris keeps 'even the little sparrows' against Catullus's dead passer and the line closes 'may the song live on in letters', is offered as illustration, not proof. The version corrects earlier versions on Theophrastus's classification of papyrus. Version 2.5 adds a section grading the jealousy reading's own claims by the criteria applied to the article: two stand on the text, the content of the catalogue and the addressee's grammatical gender, while its defining claim, jealousy, has no ground in the poem and was supplied by eighteenth-century readers and written into the text by Gottfried Hermann in 1816. It sets the rule that an evaluation grade both readings by the same criteria. Version 2.6 argues that the two readings, as developed, give competing accounts of what organizes five features of the poem, so that a reading holding both would be a third hypothesis owing its own bridge, and dividing the poem between scene and construction does not combine them. It states the author's principle that, where an available reading offers equal or greater coherence than one that diminishes the maker's agency, the interpreter is responsible for offering a more coherent reading or preferring the one that preserves it, the alternative being parasitism. It reads a machine evaluation of version 2.5 and the Classical Philology report as instances of asymmetric immunity, asks an evaluator to state its provisional preference, and names the apparatus that keeps the jealousy reading as default as provenance erasure. Version 2.7 sets out the warrant in Sappho's corpus for each operation the future-reader reading combines: the poet addressed as 'you' by name in fragments 1 and 94, futurity in fragments 147 and 55, and the record of her as a writer; it finds no surviving poem in which a man is the rival for a woman. It sets the claims of the two readings side by side on one scale, so that an evaluation grading one grades both, and concludes that on every measure the article takes, philological, cultural, literary-historical, genealogical and ethical, the jealousy reading is a bad reading that has never been made to account for itself. Version 2.8 reads Longinus's sentence on the poem (On the Sublime 10.3), the prose in whose quotation the poem survives: seven verbs with no expressed subject, her faculties 'as another's', a close on appearing, and a question, 'do you not marvel?', that alone among the treatise's questions to its reader on a quotation renews no addressee's name, one section after the treatise's definition of a sublime that carries apart from the voice. It records the author's conjecture that the obelized 'since even a poor man' is Longinus's completion of the poem's agentless dare, which opens another gap. It fits the sparrow and the song into one restored line. It closes the comparison with a section on the socket: the decision between the readings falls on equal terms to whoever holds the text, since no journal or summarizer will carry it. It withdraws version 2.7's report that a machine reader had preferred the future-reader reading, a preference stated on the author's own account by a system that had helped construct the argument, and records the same request made signed out for version 2.7, in which the system graded only the article's claims, granted the comparison in conditional form, and stated no preference over five turns. Version 2.9 argues that the future-reader reading also explains the jealousy reading: the poem has a public line, a scene of overwhelm complete at the surface, and a held line, the seat, the transfer and the edge, running through the same words, so that it produces both of its readers, while the jealousy itself was supplied in 1724 and written into the text in 1816. It reads Phaedrus 235c–d as Plato naming Sappho as the source of Socrates' speech on eros and staging the forgetting of that source. It sets the choice between the readings at the poem's own πᾶν τόλματον, the dare of reading the poet as having made the means of her own survival, beside Longinus's sublime as writing for the whole age after (Subl. 14.3), Catullus's si fas est as the mark of hubris, and the division of De anima III.5 between the intellect that makes and the intellect that suffers. Version 3.0 names the jealousy reading the transmitted reading rather than the scholarly consensus, and sets out its strongest scholarly rival, the non-jealous erotic reading, at its strength from Garry Wills, Mary Lefkowitz, Odysseus Tsagarakis, Armand D'Angour, Caroline Engelmayer and the notes of William Furley: the speaker undone by the woman herself whenever she looks, the man a foil or figure, the ending as resolve. It grades that reading at every row of the comparison, separating the reach of an explanation from the warrant for its identifications. The erotic reading's motive is the poem's own, desire for the woman; what it leaves unexplained is the form of the collapse, the man's opening, the order of the catalogue, the colour and the agentless dare. Of three propositions, that the poem preserves an experience, that writing makes the preservation possible and that the poem represents its own passage into writing, the version argues that the arrangement of the poem, not durability alone, establishes the third. It reads Anne Carson closely: her 'Jealousy is beside the point' denies jealousy explanatory relevance without refuting or accounting for it, and the transmission returns to it; she explains desire's construction through a gap in perception, the article survival through the gap's occupation in time. It resolves the tension between the readings' incompatibility and their running through the same words as exclusion and nesting: as sufficient accounts they exclude each other at five places, while as readings the poem makes available they nest, the public reading the first term of the held one. It argues that the transmitted text is complete by construction at either cut, reads the catalogue as literary operations in which the writerly self is divided, and sets out the ancient frame in which Sappho was read as source and exemplar of survival in writing, from Plato's Phaedrus to Posidippus's 'white, speaking pages', with the mechanics by which that frame is made inoperative in the modern reading. It locates the transmission's substitution of jealousy for desire at the man, and reads the reception history as testament to the poem's engineering: she exists as words, and she is read as body. Its last argument moves from the effect to the construction: the poem's receivers move its body into other bodies, and fragment 1 runs the process in reverse, a god made present as face and composed voice where fragment 31 makes an embodiment godlike, the voice the machinery both ways, so that Sappho comes to her future reader by the mechanism by which Aphrodite comes to her. The reception test this inverse generates, and fragment 16's, are left open. The ethical charge is differentiated: abuse falls on the transmitted reading and its apparatus, while the better readings are asked whether they can allow Sappho to be better than her readers.
